title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic
author: nathan-barry

excerpt: A while back, Thinking Machines published Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference, which explained why greedy decoding isn’t deterministic in production. In theory, at temperature 0 a model always picks its single most likely next token, so the same prompt gives the same answer every time. In practice, when they sent one prompt 1,000 times, they got 80 different answers.1 The problem is that floating-point addition is not associative. $(a + b) + c$ and $a + (b + c)$ can round differently. A GPU sums thousands of numbers for every token, and the order it sums them in depends on things like how many other requests are in the batch. Change the order, change the rounding, and occasionally change which token wins. Their fix was to pin the order: rewrite the kernels so that a given GPU always adds numbers in the same order, no matter what else is in the batch. That works, but only on that GPU with those kernels. An H100 and an A100 use different matrix-multiply kernels, a CPU uses different instructions entirely, and each one rounds its own way. Run the same model on all three and you still get three different answers. I always wondered, what if we just didn’t use floats? Integer addition is exact, so the order can’t matter. If every operation in the model used integers, the output should be bit-identical everywhere: any batch size, any GPU, any CPU, any vendor. Eventually I found time to work on this during a SpaceXAI hackathon. The project, DetLLM, worked well enough to become a paper at two NeurIPS 2026 workshops.2 In this post I’ll walk through why LLM inference is nondeterministic, why integers fix it, and how to run every part of an LLM (matmuls, softmax, normalization, rotary embeddings) without a single floating-point operation.
